entries.verbatim: Aristotle's lively praise of Homeric style continues, culminating with this observation: 'He makes everything move and live, and energeia is motion' (1412a.9–10). Movement and life, kinēsis and zōos, are what confer rhetorical presence.
entries.insertion_anchor: they are a *movement* (kinēsis) of the soul, a dynamic reorientation
entries.rationale: Aristotle's own equation energeia = kinēsis; converts the etymological argument into ontological doctrine.

entries.verbatim: the lectures devoted to *pathos* can be seen as a long meditation on 1378a19–21: 'The emotions are all those feelings that so change men as to affect their judgements [*kriseis*] and that are also attended by pain and pleasure.' … Heidegger grasps the emphasis on change, and therefore time. In his account of Aristotelian psychology, *kinesis* gives the authentic *Da-Charakter* to Dasein, the vital place-time of Being (287). Thus, the ontological significance of the passions lies in our capacity for change, the *Veränderlichkeit* of Being.
entries.insertion_anchor: Aristotle's claim that *pathos* is a form of *kinēsis*: a being-moved of the soul
entries.rationale: Authoritative scholarly statement that kinesis gives Dasein its Da-Charakter via the pathē.

entries.verbatim: Aristotle does not wish to deny that affections in question are motions. On the contrary, he accepts that they are. What he denies is that the soul is the proper subject of these motions. … the soul is only the terminus and the origin of motions that take place inside the body, not something that itself undergoes these motions.
entries.insertion_anchor: being pained or pleased, or thinking, are movements
entries.rationale: Best contemporary clarification of how the soul is kinetically implicated without being the substrate.

entries.verbatim: all phantasiai are motions in the soul caused by sense-perceptions. They are sensory images or imprints that can exist independently from their original source.
entries.insertion_anchor: being pained or pleased, or thinking, are movements
entries.rationale: Establishes that the resonant kinēsis is the standard Aristotelian definition of phantasia.

entries.verbatim: imagination (phantasia) must be a movement produced by sensation actively operating. Since sight (opsis) is the chief sense, the name phantasia is derived from phaos (light).
entries.rationale: The phōs etymology mirrors the user's e-mot-ion etymology — homologous derivations.

entries.verbatim: phantasmata are representations and in some sense likenesses of what they represent, they are not themselves viewed and do not look like the objects they are about. They are states of our body, bearing representational content.
entries.rationale: Direct support for the chapter's bodily-kinetic (not imagistic) reading of the resonant kinēsis.

entries.verbatim: Heidegger characterizes pathos (variously 'passion,' 'affect,' 'mood,' or 'emotion') as the very condition for the possibility of rational discourse, or logos. No cynical and crowd-pleasing addition to logos, pathos is the very substance in which propositional thought finds its objects and its motivation. Without affect our disembodied minds would have no heart, and no legs to stand on.
entries.rationale: Most economical statement of the chapter's central thesis: pathos grounds logos.

entries.verbatim: the pathē are not 'psychic experiences,' are not 'in consciousness,' but are a being-taken of human beings in their full being-in-the-world. … The so-called 'bodily state' of anxiety, joy, and so forth, are not symptoms, but also belong to the characteristic being of beings, of human beings.
entries.rationale: Agosta's translation of the same passage user already quotes from BCAP 133.

entries.verbatim: Every pathos that I experience reveals me to myself as moved in some way, positioned and posed by the things I encounter.
entries.insertion_anchor: the pathē … are the basic possibilities in which being-there itself is primarily oriented toward itself, finds itself
entries.rationale: Withy's reformulation of Heidegger's BCAP-thesis in fresh, citable English.

entries.verbatim: These πάθη … are not states pertaining to ensouled things, but are concerned with a disposition of living things in their world, in the mode of being positioned toward something, allowing a matter to matter to it.

Aristotle's Rhetoric offers alternatives for understanding emotions as social phenomena, which is something that leading humanists like Martha Nussbaum and Richard Sorabji should have remembered as they rushed toward the latest brain science.
entries.rationale: Gross gives the social-ontology framing that complements Heidegger's anti-psychologism.

entries.verbatim: Rhetoric, as a humanistic form of affordance theory, posits a situation that is not neutral but is rather 'persuasive,' threatening and promising with respect to our human being-in-the-world.
entries.rationale: Modernizes 'being-taken' into the ecological idiom of affordance.

entries.verbatim: Things get to us. They affect, afflict, strike, matter to, and move us.
entries.rationale: Compelling phenomenological framing of the central question. Note: also recurs in §1.9 E with same content.

entries.verbatim: ecology unseats the traditional locus of agency, from human action to dwelling itself. … Dwelling means the flourishing of life through attunement to the surrounding environment.

this … marks … an emotional, psychological, and attitudinal response crystallized into a moment of recognition in which everything falls into place. … This enthymizing marks an abrupt shift in perspective involving the whole person.
Once in existence the residual motion has a life of its own, it can change in character and truth-value in the way that Aristotle suggests.
entries.rationale: Direct textual warrant for the user's resonant kinēsis concept.

entries.verbatim: the definition of phantasia as 'a movement produced by sensation actively operating' (kinesis hypo tes aistheseos tes kat'energeian gignomenes). Such a secondary movement necessarily resembles sensation … the movement of phantasia evidently continues in the absence of the sensible object and the inoperancy of the sense-power.
entries.rationale: Technical Aristotelian formula for the user's resonant kinēsis.

entries.verbatim: imperfect or indefinite creatures … possess an indefinite/indeterminate kind of phantasia. Representations of touch (phantasmata) … do not remain in them, after the sense object is gone.
entries.rationale: Threshold below which residual motion fails — defines the user's contrast.

entries.verbatim: in animals other than indefinite creatures … the product of phantasia or phantasma remains in them even after the sense object is gone.
entries.rationale: Direct textual warrant for the present/absent-object distinction.

entries.verbatim: Phantasia is a type of motion that arises by actual sensation. Sensation is activated by the presence of the external object.
Phantasia will consequently be about what a sensation is about (De an. 3.3, 428b 12), even if the object is not in view.
entries.insertion_anchor: (phantasia preserves the aboutness of perception across object-removal)
entries.rationale: Phantasia preserves the aboutness of perception across object-removal.

entries.verbatim: Insofar as the human being lets something be said, he is λόγον ἔχον in a new respect. He lets something be said insofar as he hears.
When Being in a soma belongs to a living thing, then soma also belongs to the right understanding of the basic phenomenon of the pathe.

a Stimmung is like 'a melody that does not merely hover over the so-called proper being at hand of the human, but that sets the tone for such being, i.e., attunes [stimmt] and determines [bestimmt] the manner and way of its being.'

Empedocles posited a rational basis for the cosmos through underlying principles, but … this important step in logical abstraction remained phenomenological. Certainly we are given abstract principles, but these principles are always encountered.
the city's output is found to contain several extralogical ingredients, including intoxicating quantities of emotional appeal (pathos) and character appeal (ethos).
any thing which has at least one sense can feel pleasure and pain, and if so, will have appetite and hence desire (2.2, 413b22-23; 2.3, 414b4-5; 3.11, 434a2-3)
entries.insertion_anchor: the basic pleasure/pain valence co-given with *aisthēsis*
entries.rationale: Caston's compact gloss on the pleasure/pain-with-perception thesis.

entries.verbatim: I shall try to demonstrate that when we study in depth the notion of phantasia (φαντασία), as it is described in Book III of De Anima, we can realize that Aristotle speaks about three and not two kinds or grades of phantasia.
entries.rationale: Independent Aristotelian textual warrant for graded — not categorical — distinctions.

entries.verbatim: Aristotle … discriminates not two —as it is commonly argued— but three kinds or grades of phantasia: (a) Indefinite/indeterminate phantasia … (b) Sensitive phantasia … (c) Calculative, or deliberative, phantasia.
entries.rationale: Compact statement of the Aristotelian gradient that the user's 'two articulational concretions' claim adapts.

entries.verbatim: the imaginative (phantastikon) is the same as the sensitive faculty, although the imaginative and the sensitive are different in essence (einai); and since phantasia is the process set up by a sense faculty in a state of activity
entries.rationale: White's 'same-but-different-in-being' relation is the structural template for 'single ontological structure with two articulational concretions.'

entries.verbatim: Aristotle even provides a subdivision to distinguish between the calculative or deliberative imagination as it functions in human decision-making, and the non-rational imagination that is shared by the animals.
entries.rationale: Frede registers the bouleutikē/aisthētikē distinction directly.

entries.verbatim: for Aristotle to talk of a sensory phantasia would be to ascribe some (potentially motivating) content to the animal's perception, and that the animal who 'phantasizes' will not just perceive an object, but perceive it as a thing of a certain sort, a thing that could become for him an object either of pursuit or of avoidance.
entries.insertion_anchor: Basic *pathos* as affective valence or *resonant orexis* (involved position-taking, pre-propositional, 'this-as-pursue-able')
entries.rationale: The canonical scholarly statement of the perceiving-as structure.

entries.verbatim: By making phantasia the common currency among mental states rather than belief, Aristotle emphasizes a form of intentionality which is more basic than the conceptual.
entries.insertion_anchor: the pre-propositional, but not *pre-positional* hedonic tonality
entries.rationale: Pre-conceptual intentionality grounds the chapter's pre-propositional/pre-positional distinction.

entries.verbatim: I thus find myself in the midst of objects of pursuit and avoidance, liable to impact from them. They can help or hurt, uplift or upset … Not only do things show up to me as able to touch and move me in these ways, I show up to myself as vulnerable to being affected by them.
entries.insertion_anchor: the soul's already-being-disposed-toward the perceived as pursue-able or avoid-able
entries.rationale: Withy's reformulation in 2023 of perceiver-as-pursuer/avoider structure.

entries.verbatim: it seems entirely possible to mark off nows by merely perceiving them. … Aristotelian perception is perfectly able to do this by itself, without the help of intellect.
entries.insertion_anchor: Heidegger's gloss on perception as 'a *μέσον* with the character of *κριτικόν*'

entries.verbatim: we are always passively receiving perceptual stimuli; but when we actively focus on some object … the faculty of phantasia, or the phantasia-aspect of aisthēsis, is called into play.
to experience a pathos is, most basically, to be impacted and changed by the world. … some entities … are not merely changed but helped or hurt. Those are the entities that are in the world.
entries.rationale: Links §1.2's Metaphysics fourfold to the phenomenological structure.

entries.verbatim: other animals than man are thought not to have opinion (δόξα), because their desires have no deliberation. Only animals with intellect—and therefore language—have the phantasia that comes from inference.
entries.rationale: Direct warrant for the analogical/non-univocal attribution of pathos-like states to non-rational animals.

entries.verbatim: Calculative, or deliberative, phantasia (λογιστικὴ or βουλευτικὴ φαντασία) … appears only in human beings.

Phantasia in the form of sense (aisthētikē) is found, as we have said, in all animals, but deliberative phantasia only in the calculative (logistikois); for to decide whether one shall do this or that calls at once for calculation … This implies the ability to combine several images (pleionōn phantasmatōn) into one.
entries.rationale: Hawhee's translation of the DA 3.11 division of phantasia.

entries.verbatim: Only in this sense is it right to say that we feel an emotion: not as a bare affection, as a dog may be said to be angry—for emotion is not a sensory datum impinging on the senses—but by becoming aware of a phantasma that is, in turn, attended by pleasure or pain.
entries.rationale: Direct textual warrant for the analogical/non-univocal attribution.

entries.verbatim: (Same DA III.11, 434a6-15 Aristotle passage in Bowin's translation; triangulation)

Pathos is a sudden change and hence a transformation … out of a previous situation, but not a sudden change that would take its own course. Instead, it is a way of disposing oneself toward the world that stands at the same time in a possible relation to hexis.
entries.insertion_anchor: (parallel translation of Heidegger's gloss on the Rhetoric threefold)
entries.rationale: Parallel translation supplementing user's BCAP 115 quote.

entries.verbatim: if these lines are an adequate definition of emotion, this suggests that Aristotle's view is that emotions involve distinctive judgements. … 'Krisis' generally means a verdict or decision reached after considering both sides.
entries.insertion_anchor: Heidegger's gloss 'Kriseis here are not external judgments altered by emotion-from-without; they are position-takings'
entries.rationale: Philological backing for Heidegger's reading of krisis.

entries.verbatim: what seems to be needed is for Aristotle to be insisting that emotions have as an essential feature pain and pleasure that is connected in the right kind of way to the rest of the emotion. In fear, it is not merely any pain that is involved, but pain that is connected to the apparent advent of something bad.
entries.insertion_anchor: hedonic tonality (the pain or pleasure that attends the whole complex)
entries.rationale: Philological backing for the right-kind-of-pain-pleasure tonality requirement.

entries.verbatim: the Rhetoric … if the definitions were not true … would fail to provide the necessary knowledge required. … For Aristotle, a têchnê … is a disposition (hexis), which reliably produces its intended results by proceeding from true principles (EN 1140a7-10, 21-23).
entries.insertion_anchor: (defense of Rhetoric II.1 as primary ontological anchor)
entries.rationale: Substantiates the chapter's reliance on the Rhetoric II.1 definition as a primary ontological anchor (not merely endoxa).

entries.verbatim: Heidegger's penetrating but sparse remarks in Being and Time on Befindlichkeit ['affectivity'] are deepened and implemented in his reading of Aristotle's Rhetoric.
entries.rationale: Bridge between Befindlichkeit and the Rhetoric.

entries.verbatim: Aristotle's Rhetoric must be understood as the first systematic hermeneutics of the everydayness of being-with-one-another.
On this question, Martin Heidegger thinks that the history of philosophy has offered 'nothing essentially new' since Aristotle.
In the 1924 lecture Heidegger especially emphasized 'how logos had its ground in pathe.' The pathe are 'the fundamental possibilities, by which Dasein primarily orients itself, is attuned…'
entries.rationale: Gadamer's authoritative recollection of the 1924 lectures.

entries.verbatim: the pathe are not the annex of psychological events, but compose instead the ground upon which language grows and to which expressions return … This basic Being-oriented … is no knowledge, but is instead a finding-oneself
entries.rationale: Gross translation parallel to Heidegger lecture text.

entries.verbatim: Heidegger pleads against the metaphysical tradition that restricts λόγος in a unilateral way to its propositional and categorical dimension. … he interprets λόγος primarily as language, as the ability to speak, and, above all, as the capacity to discover par excellence.
the dual register of pathos (chillings/heatings vs. higher-order Rhetoric-II pathē)
entries.rationale: Disentangles a structural problem the user grapples with.

entries.verbatim: As Aristotle famously states in De Anima, emotions are 'enmattered accounts' (logoi enuloi) (DA 403a25); emotions involve both material changes in the body and a 'rich cognitive structure' of beliefs or impression (cf. Nussbaum 1996, p. 311).
entries.rationale: Direct secondary statement of the chapter's anchor thesis. Insert at opening sentence of §1.3.

entries.verbatim: the eidos of fear draws primarily upon a body's condition. The difference lies in the fact that the particular condition of the body … plays no role in mathematical inseparability, while for the pathe Being in such and such a condition is essential. Both are logoi enyloi, but in quite different senses of the term…. The eidos of the pathe is a disposition toward other humans, a Being-in-the-world.
entries.insertion_anchor: Only in *phenomenology* has this begun. No division between 'psychic' and 'bodily acts'!
entries.rationale: Extends the user's existing Heidegger-quote with the precise logoi enyloi doctrine.

entries.verbatim: Documents the 403a7 list of pathē tēs psuchēs with the explicit Greek and parallel passages.
entries.rationale: Greek-philological anchor for the pathē tēs psuchēs list.

entries.verbatim: anger or fear consists in the heart being moved in such and such a way, and thinking consists perhaps in this being moved or something else; of these modifications some arise when certain parts are moved locally, others when certain parts are altered.
entries.insertion_anchor: the shaking and the blood-rush are not symptoms of a hidden judgment
entries.rationale: Direct mechanism for the bodily-form-as-constitutive thesis.

entries.verbatim: The 'bodily state' in which anxiety (fear) or joy is expressed in facial features or physical gestures are not symptoms of hidden, underlying pathē. They are the very being of the pathē themselves — nothing is hidden … The fear is immediately available and present in the wide eyes and grimace — the joy in the laughing eyes and smile.
entries.insertion_anchor: the shaking and the blood-rush are not symptoms of a hidden judgment

entries.verbatim: Aristotle certainly thinks that spirited desire (thumos), of which anger is an expression, is painful (EE. 1225b30–31). … Certainly, Aristotle conceives of anger as an embodied phenomenon (e.g. in De Anima, Aristotle describes anger as involving 'boiling blood' around the heart (DA 403a29-b1).)

An account of emotions as pleasures and pains also seems well-placed to offer an appropriately unified account of various features of emotions. The features in question are the cognitions and consequent rational and inferential relations, the phenomenology, associated motivations, and possibly also the physiological changes involved.
entries.insertion_anchor: no analysis or explanation of emotion that reduces it to any one of these components will suffice
entries.rationale: Best contemporary statement of the multi-feature unified account.

entries.verbatim: This cycle takes up the whole of human experience; it is at once cognitive and inferential, affective and emotional, appetitive and aesthetic, ethical and normative. These layers are interconnected

Phantasia figures into Aristotle's famous definition of anger in chapter 2: 'Let anger be [defined as] desire, accompanied by [mental and physical] distress, for apparent retaliation because of an apparent slight that was directed, without justification, against oneself or those near to one' (2.2.1378a.30–32). At the heart of this definition is phainomenēs/n, one of the verbs from which phantasia is derived.
entries.rationale: Locks in the four-component compositional definition of anger.

entries.verbatim: Debating 'Emotions: hardwired or socially constructed?' is distracting because it collapses the phenomenology that is where we in fact spend most of our time. So to replace this binary debate I offer the following phenomenology of emotion … which … we can also call this … a 'rhetoric of emotion.'
entries.rationale: Modernizes the dialectician/physicist convergence as a refusal of the binary.

entries.verbatim: phantasiai … remain phenomena in their own right.
the cognitive (propositional attitude) approach to the affects is incomplete, that something essential escapes.
as one reads Empedocles' surviving fragments, it is striking how palpable and sensuous everything is. … This conception of the cosmos embraces embodiment and emplacement.
yes, I now agree, from the perspective of uncompromised humanities inquiry, there is a worthwhile science of emotion.
Because it can function apart from acceptance, moreover, it is possible to remain emotionally unaffected by its contents (3.3, 427a23-24). Belief, in contrast, affects us immediately (427a21-22).
entries.insertion_anchor: Aristotle's statement that when merely imagining we remain 'unaffected' superficially seems to be a counter-example
entries.rationale: The single most important secondary citation for §1.4 — direct gloss on user's anchor passage.

entries.verbatim: Being in such a state, he continues, is something 'like viewing fgures in a painting' (ὥσπερ ἂν εἰ θεώμενοι ἐν γραφῇ, 427b23–24) insofar as it needn't produce an emotional reaction in us, even when what is depicted is arousing or terrifying.
entries.insertion_anchor: Aristotle's statement that when merely imagining we remain 'unaffected' superficially seems to be a counter-example
entries.rationale: Caston's direct gloss on the user's anchor passage (DA 427b21-24).

entries.verbatim: Aristotle distinguishes this mode of phantasia from opinion (doxa), arguing, 'it is not in our power to form opinions as we will' (427b). Instead, 'when we form an opinion that something is threatening or frightening, we are immediately affected by it' (427b). Opinion's resistance to the conscious control of the will affords it an urgent and unpredictable affective power.
entries.insertion_anchor: doxa, for rational animals, serves as not only a condition but also as a cognitive gate
entries.rationale: Direct paraphrase of the user's claim re: involuntary doxa befalling the agent.

entries.verbatim: Furthermore, whenever we believe something terrible or fearsome, we immediately have an emotion, and likewise if it is something encouraging. Whereas in the case of appearance, we are in the kind of state we would be if seeing terrible or encouraging things in a painting.
entries.insertion_anchor: Further, when we think something to be fearful or threatening, emotion is immediately produced
entries.rationale: Alternate translation of DA 427b21-24 providing triangulation with Caston.

entries.verbatim: Aristotle's point is that belief is sufficient for emotion, whereas phantasia is not. Taken together, this strongly suggests (though it is not explicit) that Aristotle's position is that belief is also necessary for emotion.
entries.insertion_anchor: *doxa*, for rational animals, serves as not only a condition but also as a cognitive gate
entries.rationale: Doxa as necessary condition for emotion.

entries.verbatim: the goal of rhetorical practice is phantasia with pistis, but pistis cannot exist without doxa … in the Rhetoric Aristotle elides the possibility of phantasia without doxa, and this sufficiently accounts for what seems superficially like emotion without belief.
Fortenbaugh (1975) and Nussbaum (1994) have discussed Aristotle's cognitive conception of the emotions. … Doxa, Fortenbaugh states, is the efficient cause of emotion (1975, 15).
Aristotle's assertion about fear in this passage is very close to what he says in Rhetoric II.5, 1382b33, 'those who believe they might suffer something necessarily are afraid.'
entries.insertion_anchor: Heidegger's gloss 'the one who is brought into fear must once believe'

entries.verbatim: a slight is the actualisation of an opinion [energeia tês doxês] about what appears [to be] of no worth at all. (Rhet. 1378b10).… anger responds only to the particular expression (energeia) of that attitude. Idle attitudes or opinions alone are not sufficient for anger.
entries.insertion_anchor: the cognitive content is the perceived slight

entries.verbatim: DA 433a10-22 calls phantasia a kind of thinking: as doxa, it is a critical faculty (even if not a full i.e., independent, one); but, significantly, in contrast to doxa, it does not necessarily carry pistis (DA 428a20-24)
Phantasia thus stands midway between these different powers. It is more basic than the intellectual powers, extending throughout the animal kingdom, while also being capable of error.
entries.insertion_anchor: The bare *phantasma*… leaves the soul unaffected
entries.rationale: Phantasia as midway between intellectual powers.

entries.verbatim: an inferential response on the part of the audience typically does not feel like a deduction so much as a perception, a moment of recognition or realization, colored by emotional responses and moral judgments.
entries.insertion_anchor: the speed with which emotion follows *doxa*---'immediately'---suggests that the *doxastic* component of emotion is closer to perceptual recognition than to discursive inference
entries.rationale: Inferential response feels like perception — supports the perceptual-recognition gloss.

entries.verbatim: 1. To have an emotion is to experience pain, pleasure or both. 2. The pain and pleasure involved in having an emotion is … intentional and representational: it is pain/pleasure at the emotion's object or 'target' and involves that target being represented in ways that give 'grounds' for the particular emotion experienced.
entries.insertion_anchor: each emotion specifies a cognitive content, a hedonic valence, and (in most cases) a conative component
entries.rationale: Dow's compact summary of emotion's intentional-representational structure.

entries.verbatim: Every animal that has belief also has phantasia, since belief is a kind of accepting or taking something to be the case (427b24-26), and there is no acceptance without phantasia
It is not possible to believe just anything … Phantasia, in contrast, allows us to conjure up images freely, independent of our views about what is true (427b17-20).
Phantasia is a faculty of the soul, the imaginative (φανταστικόν), that is placed between sensation (αἴσθησις) and thought (διάνοια).
entries.rationale: Phantasia as faculty between aisthēsis and dianoia.

entries.verbatim: Phantasia, according to Aristotle, is an affection (πάθος) and 'this affection is in our own power whenever we wish'. So, it is up to us to imagine, but it is not up to us to believe
entries.rationale: Voluntariness of phantasia vs involuntariness of belief.

entries.verbatim: Aristotle puts phantasia in a complex relationship with emotion (pathos) … Phantasia … is called a pathos, 'an affection that lies in our power whenever we choose' (427b).
(Catalogues fear/shame/honor as phantasia-grounded definitions in the Rhetoric)
When men are angered, they are not victims of some totally irrational force. … their behavior is intelligent and cognitive in the sense that it is grounded upon a belief which may be criticized.

the participles emphasise that the definition explains how things appear to the angry person, how he takes things to be. … it is intrinsic to anger that one thinks one has been slighted, but not that one has actually been slighted.
entries.insertion_anchor: (§1.6: Emotion follows not judgment (krisis) but appearance-laden belief)

entries.verbatim: anger involves cognitive content, a set of beliefs or impressions about the world. The angry person takes himself to have been undeservedly slighted, and therefore come to desire what he thinks will constitute revenge.

Performative. As we have seen, William Reddy offers 'I love you' as an emotive that does not merely describe some preexisting condition, it instantiates the emotion and it does so unpredictably because the outcome is not certain.

Pitying Colin … might be the painful judgement that he is suffering undeservedly … But additionally, for the judgement to be genuinely painful probably requires the deployment of some specific bodily apparatus
this passage seems to be a rather general observation about emotional experience, and as such suggests that Aristotle took it to be simply obvious that emotions involve beliefs.
δόξα is the mode in which living knows from out of itself. … δόξα is the mode in which we have living there in its everydayness.
δόξα, in short, provides the basis of and the impetus to conversation … δόξα is the source of 'the genuine orientedness of being-with-one-another-in-the-world.'
entries.rationale: Doxa as source of being-with orientation.

entries.verbatim: object → perception (alteration) → pleasure and pain / desire (thermic alteration). The object causes perception, which is itself an alteration, and this in turn causes thermic alteration, heating or chilling, which corresponds to the feeling of pleasure or pain as well as to the appetite or revulsion.

entries.verbatim: Alteration is caused by phantasiai and sense-perceptions and thoughts. … phantasia and thinking have the power of the actual things. entries.verbatim: Phantasia, or thought accompanied by phantasia, works by presenting the animal with the form or essence of its object … The forms presented by phantasia were called the forms 'of the pleasant or painful' (701h21), or, equivalently, 'of that which produces the affections' (703h19-20).
